s: Maqabis, a chief of Moab, joins with the nations, invades Israel and destroys Jerusalem, then returns home in triumph.
A prophet warns Maqabis that God will punish him. Maqabis repents in sackcloth and ashes.
God forgives Maqabis. He removes the idols from his house and keeps God's law. God saved Israel through the judges whenever they cried out.
God saved Israel through Joshua, Gideon, Samson, Deborah and Judith. Maqabis brings offerings and tithes like the Jews and lives in peace.
Maqabis dies and his sons keep his ways, caring for the poor. The Chaldeans live without law.
The priests of Tseerutsaydan's idols try to make the sons of Maqabis sacrifice. Brought before the king, they refuse and rebuke him for boasting in the work of his hands.
The sons of Maqabis warn the king of Gehenna and vanish. Trembling, he looks for their bodies to bury them, but God has hidden them.
The king, like the iron kingdom in Daniel's vision, crushes the nations in his pride. God humbles such enemies, as he did the kings Joshua defeated.
Man is dust and should not boast. Satan led Adam astray, but God raises the dead and keeps the righteous.
Kings are told not to follow Satan. The story of Balaam, who could not curse those whom God had blessed.
Moses in his meekness prayed for the people. The making of the tabernacle. Rebels will perish like Korah.
Woe to the mighty of Israel for their pride. God forgives those who trust him. A proud king perishes, and his land is plundered and burned.
The five sons of Maqabis refuse to eat meat sacrificed to idols and give their bodies to death, trusting in the resurrection.
Against the Sadducees and others who deny the resurrection of the dead.
On the day of judgment those who denied the resurrection will grieve, and fire will fall on them.
Nails and hair grow back when cut: a sign of the resurrection of soul and body together.
A grain of wheat must break before it bears fruit. So the dead will rise.
Those who deny the resurrection deceive themselves. All die in Adam, and all will rise.
A lament to the earth and to death, which swallow the great and the beautiful. At the trumpet the dead will rise.
Every deed will be revealed before God. Angels of darkness take the souls of sinners and angels of light the souls of the righteous.
Where are those who gathered wealth by violence? Those who do God's will shall rejoice in his kingdom for ever.
i: 2 Meqabyan is the second of the three Ethiopian books of Meqabyan, which are not the books of Maccabees in the Catholic Bible. It opens with another Maqabis, a king of Moab who once fought against Israel and destroyed Jerusalem, then turned to the God of Israel and taught his household to keep his law.

Much of the book is preaching: on why God punishes sin and rewards the faithful, on the kings of Israel who sinned and were judged, on Job and the patience of the righteous, and on the certain hope of the resurrection. It closes with the end of the persecuting king Tseerutsaydan.
What to expect: 21 short chapters, more sermon than story. The Catholic Church does not count it among the books of the Bible.
